newsitem.title: USA: Firm harnesses buying power for small business.
newsitem.headline: Firm harnesses buying power for small business.

text.p: When Big Business goes shopping, it can depend on volume discounts just about all the time.

But small businesses strapped for cash usually are left buying products at whatever price is offered. They don't have the leverage to demand a better deal or the time to search out a range of competitive offerings.
One small Sacramento, Calif.-based company started by two women wants to change that.

The Business Equation's concept channels the buying power of small companies so that they can win volume discounts from vendors in everthing from long-distance telephone services to office products and computer cables to workers compensation insurance.

Essentially, Business Equation becomes a shopper for small business, searching out the best deal, and in the process becomes a sales agent for a vendor. It gets a discount for goods and services based on the number of its members, getting prices usually unavailable to a small firm.
Although it is the go-between that links seller and buyer, it doesn't buy any of the goods itself. It simply arranges the relationship and the terms of the purchase.

"We're not the cheapest of the cheap but what we do offer is the highest quality at extremely competitive pricing," said Judy Wallace, co-founder and co-president of the company with Joyce Axtell. "We're a sophisticated purchasing agent."

Many volume purchasers charge their participants, or members, a fee in order to get the discounted goods. The Business Equation does something else: it makes its money from the rebates it receives from a vendor based on sales and does not charge its participants a penny.
For instance, if an office supply company sells more than $1 million worth of goods to Business Equation participants, the business will receive a percentage of those sales as a rebate or commission.
It keeps a portion and passes on the rest to sales agents who sign up more participants for the programme, increasing its size, winning better volume discounts, and generating more sales and rebates.

Currently, vendors range from Office Depot, for supplies; Cable & Wireless, for long-distance services; UniGlobe, for travel services; and Intercare, for workers compensation insurance. It is negotating to provide a medical plan for its participants.
Passing on sales leads from its participants, Wallace said vendors close on 78 percent of all contacts.

The Business Equation was started in 1992 by a venture capital group, the Technology Funding Venture Partners, in San Mateo, Calif., to offer volume discounts to the largely high-technology companies it financed.
Wallace said she got the idea for the business after renegotiating a contract for the group from Office Depot and realising that she could win rebates if her purchases were larger.

From that realisation, the business was born. Wallace and Axtell bought out the company from the Technology Venture Fund in 1995 and then began expanding, signing up vendors and small business participants on the West Coast.

It has been adding new participants at a growth rate of just 50 percent per quarter for the past year and a half and now has more than 550 members throughout the West Coast. Recent expansions include North Carolina and the Southwest.
Seeking to expand further by adding sales agents and improving its internal office computer system, the company is in the process of negotiating with a group of investors to fund its expansion.
The computer system will allow it to track the buying habits of its participants -- which it could share with vendors to boost sales -- and pursue a national expansion.
